bug_semantics: picklescan treated a pickle as infected only when an extracted GLOBAL/STACK_GLOBAL pair matched its finite dangerous-global denylist. A cloudpickle payload could therefore serialize an attacker-controlled function whose bytecode calls getattr(builtins, "eval"): the pickle exposed only cloudpickle reconstruction helpers and types.CodeType, none of which were dangerous entries, so scanning reported no dangerous issue although unpickling reconstructed and invoked executable attacker-controlled code.
flaw_origin: The flaw originated in the first scanner implementation: c1d5abdcc740e0d08a0d12d015d08e1e6f29a67e introduced global extraction followed by an exact finite-module/name lookup and incremented issues_count only for matches. That architecture made unlisted callable reconstruction primitives a clean bypass from the scanner's inception; later refactors preserved the mechanism rather than introducing it.
ai_marker: absent: the BIC commit object names human author and committer Matthieu Maitre <mmaitre314@users.noreply.github.com> and its message is only "Implement Pickle scanner"; it has no Co-Authored-By, Generated-with, bot identity, or other AI trailer/marker.
evidence: The first-party advisory https://github.com/mmaitre314/picklescan/security/advisories/GHSA-9m3x-qqw2-h32h describes the getattr(builtins, "eval") cloudpickle PoC, affected versions <1.0.1, and patched version 1.0.1. `git show c1d5abdcc740e0d08a0d12d015d08e1e6f29a67e -- src/picklescan/scanner.py` shows the new src/picklescan/scanner.py:13-23 finite `_suspicious_globals` table and lines 83-87 lookup/increment logic; `git log --all --reverse -S'_suspicious_globals.get(g[0])' -- src/picklescan/scanner.py` identifies c1d5abdcc740e0d08a0d12d015d08e1e6f29a67e as the first writer. `git ls-tree -r --name-only 6a76b8c3ac67dc04181e600614ecf2a423cca326 -- src/picklescan/scanner.py` returns no path, while `git diff --name-status` from that parent to the BIC reports `A src/picklescan/scanner.py`, directly proving parent absence. `git cat-file -p c1d5abdcc740e0d08a0d12d015d08e1e6f29a67e` supplies the one parent, human author/committer, subject, and no trailers. `git show 173c8f2a869ea9b69b543477525ec70611c3c6f4` shows the direct fix adding cloudpickle.cloudpickle reconstruction helpers and types.CodeType to `_unsafe_globals` plus exploit fixtures/assertions. Tag ancestry shows c1d5abdcc740e0d08a0d12d015d08e1e6f29a67e is already in v0.0.2; `git tag --contains 173c8f2a869ea9b69b543477525ec70611c3c6f4` begins at v1.0.1 (not v1.0.0), and v1.0.1 resolves to descendant 4d9bc9cd34bca8672dad3481cd4556d5ba747156, matching the advisory boundary.
reasoning: The attack is not a parser evasion: the scanner successfully sees globals, but cloudpickle moves the dangerous eval behavior into reconstructed CodeType/function state, leaving only helper globals that the denylist did not classify as dangerous. The smallest causal commit is therefore the original commit that both created the scanner and established the exact-match denylist as the condition for an infected result. The later library split, refactors, and denylist expansions only carried that design forward, so they are not BICs. Its immediate parent lacks the scanner file entirely, proving the vulnerable mechanism absent there. The BIC precedes the earliest inspected affected tag v0.0.2, the direct remediation lands after v1.0.0 and is contained by v1.0.1, and the fix specifically blocks the globals emitted by the advisory PoC. Because only the BIC commit object controls attribution and that object has exclusively human identities with no AI marker, the closed verdict is NOT_AI.
